evidence_quotes.quote: Additionally, approximately two-thirds of the research participants rely on household groundwater wells (as opposed to municipal public water) and thus were involved in groundwater testing due to unconventional drilling and fracturing in their counties.

Even in places where water is abundant, as in West Virginia, water insecurity can be an everyday reality for individuals in rural areas who are dependent on water wells and are not connected to city water.

This regulation does not safeguard water from contamination, but it aims to protect land owners by instituting presumed liability to oil and gas companies if water contamination occurs due to gas well drilling.
We based this article on 30 semi-structured in-depth interviews conducted between April and July 2018 with stakeholders in eight northwestern West Virginia counties.

We do not quantify or measure the range of emotions produced due to water insecurity, but instead focus on how uncertainties and power injustices produce a particular form of water insecurity: water aﬀect manifested through the emotional and subjective experience of water.

criterion_notes.c1: No. The study does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access. It examines rural residents relying on unregulated private domestic groundwater wells (not connected to municipal water) facing environmental groundwater contamination threats from unconventional shale gas hydraulic fracturing, explicitly bracketing out Jepson's 'water access' dimension to focus on 'water affect' (emotional and subjective experiences of water contamination risk; Exclusion Criterion 7).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: yes — the paper examines oil-and-gas environmental regulation, specifically West Virginia Code 22-6A-18 (2013 Natural Gas Horizontal Well Control Act) governing contractor-administered pre-drilling baseline water quality testing and operator presumed liability within 1,500 feet and 6 months, well-pad setback distances, common-law severed mineral rights dominance, non-disclosure agreements, and Safe Drinking Water Act exemptions. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: no — these rules govern extractive-industry pollution monitoring and tort/remediation liability for contaminating private groundwater wells, not a rule-type mechanism (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariffs, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure) directly governing access to water or sanitation services.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Qualitative empirical case study drawing on 30 semi-structured in-depth interviews conducted between April and July 2018 across eight northwestern West Virginia counties, analyzed using NVivo 12 with provisional coding and two participatory member-checking sessions.
criterion_notes.c4: No. The study's reported outcome is 'water affect'—emotional and mental stress, anxiety over delayed/incomplete contractor water quality tests, fear of losing home equity, and perceived epistemic injustice surrounding groundwater contamination from hydraulic fracturing—rather than an outcome measuring water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or service exclusion (anecdotal accounts of contaminated private well water and company remediation 'water buffalos' concern environmental pollution damages to private self-supply wells).
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Population and unit of analysis (individual/household rural stakeholders in eight West Virginia counties, n = 30), exposure (hydraulic fracturing proximity and WV Code 22-6A-18 baseline water testing/presumed liability regime), outcome (water affect / emotional distress and perceived injustice), and study design (qualitative interview-based case study) are clearly identified.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English.

study_design: Qualitative case study using 30 semi-structured in-depth interviews and member checking
population_and_sample: 30 stakeholders (surface and/or mineral owners, concerned citizens, and representatives of statewide oil-and-gas or landowner organizations; approximately two-thirds relying on private household groundwater wells) across eight rural counties in northwestern West Virginia
exposure: Unconventional shale gas hydraulic fracturing and associated oil-and-gas environmental regulation, specifically contractor-conducted baseline groundwater quality testing and presumed-liability rules under West Virginia Code 22-6A-18
outcome: Water affect: emotional and mental stress, anxiety, distrust, fear of property-value loss, and perceived epistemic injustice regarding potential or actual private well water contamination
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic). Although empirical (30 qualitative interviews), this critical water-geography paper investigates industrial environmental pollution threats to unregulated private domestic groundwater wells from shale gas hydraulic fracturing and residents' resulting psychosocial/emotional distress ('water affect'). It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1 = no; Exclusion Criterion 7), the legal/regulatory regime analyzed (WV Code 22-6A-18 baseline water quality testing and oil-and-gas operator presumed pollution liability) regulates extractive-industry contamination damages rather than service-access rules under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification (c2 = no), and the outcome analyzed is emotional distress and epistemic injustice around groundwater quality testing rather than a water or sanitation service access outcome (c4 = no).
